A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Return-Aligned Decision Transformer (RADT). Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions and relocations.

before.justification: V3 reports original MuJoCo, Atari and AntMaze evaluations, component ablations and computational-cost measurements in Section 5 and Appendices B and D.

after.justification: V5 retains original benchmark and ablation results and reports additional return-to-go trajectory and adaptive-scaling analyses in Section 5 and Appendix A.

M1.justification: The split return/state-action sequences, SeqRA attention and adaptive scaling, StepRA transformations, training losses and inference procedure remain unchanged. V5's Section 4.3 and new StepRA illustration explain the component arrangement already shown in v3; the changed experimental layer count belongs to E3.

E1.justification: Both evaluate the same four MuJoCo locomotion tasks and dataset variants, four Atari games, and AntMaze umaze/umaze-diverse tasks. The added trajectory analysis uses an existing evaluation environment. Human-motion and heterogeneous-agent examples expand motivation, without adding evaluated tasks.

E2.justification: The return-maximization comparison narrows substantially: v3 Table 2 includes CQL, DT, DC and ODT, whereas v5 Table 4 retains only DT and DC. This removes both value-based and online-transformer comparators from that experiment. The primary alignment comparison retains DT, StARformer and DC.

E3.justification: V5 reports substantial setting revisions: MuJoCo/AntMaze warmup changes from 100,000 to 10,000 steps, hopper-medium uses two layers instead of three, and Atari maximum epochs increase from 5 to 15 while gradient clipping changes from 0.1 to 1.0. Attention analysis switches from walker2d-medium to ant-medium-replay, and timing switches from hopper-medium to hopper-medium-replay. These are reported changes, without establishing that every retained experiment was rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained SeqRA/StepRA ablations, v5 Appendix A.2 tests removal of adaptive scaling in both MuJoCo and Atari. Figure 3 and Section 5.4 add within-episode return-to-go trajectories to examine behavioral adjustment and overshooting. These analyses separately test the contribution of scaling and the dynamics underlying return alignment.

E5.justification: The established three-seed reporting practice remains. V5 adds per-timestep means and standard errors over 100 episodes for Figure 3. Its ablation captions specify normalization of the mean and standard error, replacing v3's mean-and-variance wording, although v3's main prose already mentioned standard error. Increased seed counts are not established.

E6.justification: V5 adds trajectory findings, adaptive-scaling ablation entries and per-task aggregate-error tables. Existing results also change: Seaquest without StepRA changes from 0.92 to 0.81, and hopper-medium maximization changes from 90.0±4.83 to 93.7±1.95 alongside its revised model configuration. Numerous ablation uncertainties change. Timing results of 450/562 seconds become 363/466 seconds under a different dataset split, so these are not same-setting speed improvements.

T1.justification: The finite-horizon MDP assumptions, return-to-go definition, attention mathematics, alignment objective and aligner equations remain equivalent. V5 displays the existing return-to-go formula separately and reindexes an equivalent attention sum; it adds no theorem, proof or substantive mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: The principal RADT contributions remain, while the introduction narrows its comparison claim from existing offline RL approaches to DT-based models. However, v3's errors reduced to 54.9% and 34.4% of DT's error become reductions of those percentages in v5. This changes the quantitative claim and conflicts with v5 Section 5.3's 44.6% and 65.5% reductions.

C2.justification: V5 interprets the new trajectories as evidence of adaptive action adjustment and the scaling ablation as evidence of improved integration of return information. It adds a rationale for split-specific normalization and extends the existing encoder explanation into a qualification about high-target Pong performance. Dataset-bias and computational-cost limitations were already present.

D1.justification: V5 newly identifies the public DT codebase as RADT's implementation basis, specifies A100 training hardware for MuJoCo and Atari, and discloses Atari context lengths of 50 for Pong and 30 otherwise. Conversely, v3's maximization target-return inputs in Table 7 and sinusoidal-position-encoding disclosures disappear. Baseline code links remain unchanged.

R1.justification: Application positioning is substantially revised: playtesting and traffic-simulation literature gives way to references on behavior-diverse game agents, heterogeneous crowds and human-motion generation. Related work also replaces Liu and Abbeel's agentic-transformer reference with Wang et al.'s critic-guided decision transformer. The central positioning relative to DT, StARformer and DC remains.

P1.justification: V5 extensively rewrites the introduction and method explanations, organizes motivation into three application examples, introduces a numbered contribution list and consistently distinguishes return-to-go terminology. It adds a dedicated component-arrangement subsection and reorganizes experimental discussion and appendices. This exceeds localized wording edits.

P2.justification: The opening results chart becomes an application schematic, with its summaries split and moved into the appendix. V5 adds trajectory and StepRA figures and summary/ablation tables, redraws architecture and attention displays, and transposes the MuJoCo plot grids. V3's Atari actual-return plot and maximization target-input table disappear. Typography and table layouts also change extensively.

improvement.justification: V5 strengthens mechanistic evidence through scaling ablations and trajectory analysis, and makes results easier to inspect through summary tables. However, it removes target inputs needed to reproduce retained maximization experiments and introduces conflicting percentage-reduction claims and inconsistent hopper uncertainty in Tables 3 and 5 (0.13 versus 0.24). These gains in explanation and evidence coexist with losses in reproducibility and reporting reliability, leaving the overall net direction unclear.
